objectives: Distinguish L4 vs L7 load balancing.
Apply consistent hashing for sticky connections.

slides.title: L4 vs L7 load balancing
slides.body:
**Load balancing** is the practice of distributing incoming network traffic across multiple backend servers so no single node becomes a bottleneck. Two distinct layers address very different problems.

**L4 (transport layer)** — balance at the TCP/UDP level. The load balancer sees only IP addresses and ports; it cannot read the HTTP payload. This makes L4 extremely fast — capable of handling millions of connections per second with microsecond overhead. Tools: **AWS Network Load Balancer (NLB)**, **HAProxy** in `tcp` mode, and **Google Maglev** (published 2016, uses consistent hashing plus Equal-Cost Multi-Path routing, ECMP, to achieve line-rate packet forwarding). Maglev was designed to replace hardware load balancers inside Google's datacenters and processes packets in software at near-wire speed.

**L7 (application layer)** — balance at the HTTP/gRPC level. The load balancer terminates the TCP connection, reads request headers and URL path, applies routing logic, then proxies to a backend. This costs roughly 10× the per-request overhead of L4 but enables powerful features: route `/api/v2/*` to a new service, route by the `X-User-Region` header, inject observability headers, perform TLS termination, implement circuit breaking, or enforce rate limits. Tools: **AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB)**, **HAProxy** in `http` mode, **NGINX** (originally released 2004 by **Igor Sysoev** as a high-performance reverse proxy), and **Envoy** (open-sourced by **Lyft** in 2016, created by **Matt Klein**, now a **Cloud Native Computing Foundation** graduated project). Envoy is the data-plane of choice for service meshes such as **Istio** and **AWS App Mesh**.

**Reverse proxy** is the structural pattern underlying all L7 load balancers: the proxy sits in front of origin servers, accepts client connections, and forwards requests. This is distinct from a forward proxy (which proxies on behalf of clients, not servers).

Production topology: Anycast IP at the network edge routes packets via ECMP to a tier of L4 load balancers, which distribute TCP connections to regional L7 load balancers, which inspect HTTP and route to microservice pods. Each layer adds capability at a cost in latency and complexity.

slides.title: Connection distribution algorithms
slides.body:
Choosing the right distribution algorithm is the core engineering decision in load-balancer configuration. The wrong algorithm causes hotspots, session loss, or cache-busting.

**Round-robin**: connections are distributed in strict rotation — backend 1, backend 2, backend 3, back to 1. Zero state required. Optimal for stateless services where every request is equally expensive. Default for most L7 load balancers.

**Weighted round-robin**: each backend gets a weight proportional to its capacity. A backend with weight 3 receives 3 requests per cycle; a new or underpowered node gets weight 1. Useful during canary deploys — send 5 % of traffic to the new version by assigning it weight 1 among weight-19 backends.

**Least connections**: route each new connection to the backend currently holding the fewest active connections. Superior to round-robin when connection durations vary widely (e.g., a long-lived WebSocket alongside fast REST calls). Requires the load balancer to maintain per-backend connection counts.

**IP hash / sticky sessions**: hash the client's source IP to a backend index. The same client always reaches the same backend. Useful for stateful protocols, but fails when NAT hides many clients behind one IP (all traffic concentrates on one backend).

**Consistent hashing**: map both requests and backends onto a hash ring. Each request is served by the first backend clockwise on the ring. Adding or removing one backend moves only $K/(N+1)$ keys on average (versus nearly all keys under modulo hashing). First described by **David Karger**, **Eric Lehman**, **Tom Leighton**, **Rina Panigrahy**, **Matthew Levine**, and **Daniel Lewin** (MIT, 1997). Dominant in CDNs, distributed caches (Memcached, Redis Cluster), and database sharding.

**Power of Two Random Choices**: instead of scanning all backends (expensive) or picking blindly (round-robin), pick **two** backends at random and route to the less-loaded one. **Michael Mitzenmacher** proved in 2001 (*The Power of Two Choices in Randomized Load Balancing*, IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems) that this reduces the maximum load from $O(\log N / \log \log N)$ (random) to $O(\log \log N)$ (power of two) — an exponential improvement in balance with a single extra sample. Adopted by Nginx and Envoy as `least_request` with random peer selection.

**DNS-based load balancing and anycast**: return multiple A/AAAA records from DNS; clients pick one (often randomly). Used by CDNs and large services (Google, Cloudflare). Anycast assigns the same IP to multiple geographic nodes; BGP routing naturally directs each client to the topographically nearest node.

**The thundering herd problem**: when a cached resource expires or a backend recovers from downtime, thousands of clients simultaneously send requests to the origin — overwhelming it before it stabilises. Mitigations: staggered TTLs, probabilistic early revalidation (cache recomputes before expiry), and request coalescing (the load balancer collapses concurrent identical requests into one upstream fetch).

slides.title: Health checks, connection draining, and sticky sessions
slides.body:
A load balancer is only as reliable as its ability to detect and isolate failed backends. Three operational mechanisms make this work in production.

**Health checks** are periodic probes the load balancer sends to each backend. There are three levels:
- **TCP health check**: attempt to open a TCP connection. Cheap and fast; catches a dead process but not a live-yet-broken one.
- **HTTP health check**: `GET /healthz` and inspect the HTTP status code (and optionally the response body). Catches application-layer failures — a backend that accepts TCP but returns 500s for every real request.
- **gRPC health check**: uses the standard gRPC Health Checking Protocol (defined in the gRPC specification) where the service implements `grpc.health.v1.Health/Check`. Appropriate for gRPC-only services.

Common knobs: **interval** (time between probes, typically 5–10 s), **timeout** (time to wait per probe, typically 2–3 s), and **threshold** (consecutive failures before marking unhealthy, typically 2–3). A backend marked unhealthy is immediately removed from the rotation; it is re-added only after a configurable number of consecutive successful checks. Faster detection reduces mean-time-to-recovery but risks false positives during transient network blips.

**Connection draining** (also called *graceful shutdown* or *deregistration delay* in AWS parlance) ensures that in-flight requests complete before a backend is removed. When a backend is marked unhealthy or deregistered, the load balancer stops sending new connections but allows existing ones up to a drain timeout (typically 30–60 s) to finish. Without draining, a rolling deploy terminates connections mid-stream and users see errors.

**Sticky sessions** (also called *session affinity*) ensure that a given client is always routed to the same backend. Implementations:
- **Cookie-based stickiness** (L7 only): the load balancer injects a special cookie (e.g., `AWSALB` or `SERVERID`) on the first response; subsequent requests bearing that cookie are routed to the same backend. HAProxy implements this as `cookie SERVERID insert indirect`.
- **Source-IP stickiness** (L4 or L7): hash the client IP. Breaks badly under NAT.
- **Application-managed sessions**: the backend stores session state in a shared store (Redis, a database) so any backend can serve any request — making stickiness unnecessary. This is the preferred architecture for horizontally scaled systems.

The tension: stickiness undermines the load-balancing goal (even distribution) in exchange for session continuity. The industry trend is to eliminate the need for stickiness via shared-state stores, leaving the load balancer free to route optimally.

question.question: Derive consistent-hashing key movement
question.goal: Ring of $N$ servers + $K$ keys. Add one server. How many keys move?

steps.prompt: Consistent hashing: each server gets a position on the ring (often multiple via virtual nodes). New server takes over keys in its 'arc' — keys between its position + the previous server's. With random positioning, the new server's arc is about $1/(N+1)$ of total.
hints: New server claims fraction $1/(N+1)$ of total.
steps.reveal: $K/(N+1)$ keys move. Independent of total key count $K$.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{K/(N+1) \text{ keys move when adding 1 server}}$$ The reason consistent hashing dominates in CDNs, caches, distributed DBs. Hash-modulo would move ~all keys; consistent hashing moves only the new server's share.

question.question: You're load-balancing a microservice fleet. Some services need sticky sessions (state on a specific node); others are stateless. Best architecture:
options: Use sticky sessions for everything — simpler.
Use L7 LB with cookie-based stickiness for stateful services + round-robin for stateless.
question.explanation: L7 LB can route stateful requests via cookie (sticky) + stateless requests via round-robin. Different services configured differently. L4 doesn't see cookies; sticky-everything wastes resource utilization on stateless services. Hybrid is the production pattern.

hints: You need different policies per service.
L7 sees application-layer data (cookies, headers) needed for cookie-based routing.
slides.workedSolution: L7 LB inspects HTTP, can route via cookie (sticky) or path/method (stateless). Different services in the same fleet can have different routing policies. L4 doesn't see cookies; sticky-everywhere wastes load-balancing benefits on stateless services. Production: L7 with per-service config.

question.question: A hot spot in consistent hashing
question.prompt: Your consistent-hashing-based cache has one node receiving 5× the QPS of the average. Walk through why this can happen + what to do about it.
Explain in two or three sentences why modern microservice architectures heavily layer L7 load balancers (e.g., Envoy as service mesh).
question.rubric: Mentions that L7 LBs can do circuit breaking, retries, rate limiting, observability, etc., all without app code changes; the service mesh pattern (sidecar L7 proxy per pod) extends this to every service in a microservice cluster.
